# Food insecurity is associated with dysfunctional eating behaviors among adults in Puerto Rico

**Authors:** Wanqing Xu; Andrea López-Cepero; Husn June O’Neill; Anna Plym; S. Bryn Austin; Josiemer Mattei

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 2Department of Nutrition, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 3Department of Medical Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Karolinska Institute, Stockholm, Sweden | 4Department of Surgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 5Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 6Division of Adolescent and Young Adult Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

To examine the association between food insecurity and dysfunctional eating behaviors among adults in Puerto Rico.

Data from 865 participants were obtained from baseline interviews from the PROSPECT cohort. The association between food insecurity and emotional eating (EE) and uncontrolled eating (UE) (categorized as no/moderate/high) was examined using multinomial logistic models. Potential mediation by perceived stress was explored.

The prevalence of food insecurity was 20.3%. Compared with food-secure adults, food-insecure adults had higher odds of both moderate EE (OR: 1.91; 95% CI: 1.18, 3.09) and high EE (OR: 2.85; 95% CI: 1.75, 4.64), and both moderate UE (OR: 1.78; 95% CI: 0.91, 3.50) and high UE (OR: 3.28; 95% CI: 1.70, 6.33). Perceived stress slightly attenuated these associations.

Food insecurity was associated with higher likelihood of engaging in dysfunctional eating behaviors. Interventions alleviating food insecurity or stress might help adults sustain healthy eating behaviors.

## INTRODUCTION

Food insecurity (FI), defined as a condition of limited or uncertain access to adequate food, is a major public health problem, with a negative impact on multiple life domains including nutrition-related chronic diseases such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.1, 2 In the United States (US), FI is present in 12% of households and disproportionately affects Latino households.3 In comparison, the prevalence of FI is high in Puerto Rico (PR), present in approximately one-third of adults.4 Recent events in PR, including political instability, natural disasters, economic downturn, and the COVID-19 pandemic, may have exacerbated FI.5, 6 Residents of PR also experience a high burden of nutrition-related chronic diseases — 32.5% of the population has obesity and 16.7% has type 2 diabetes.7

Evidence suggests a positive association between FI and dysfunctional eating behaviors, in several populations.8–12 Two behaviors are of particular interest for FI: emotional eating (EE), defined as the tendency to eat in response to negative emotions, and uncontrolled eating (UE), defined as the tendency to overeat with the feeling of being out of control.12 Potential mechanisms linking FI and EE/UE include unhealthy compensatory behaviors (such as fasting, eating very little food, and skipping meals), hunger triggers, binge episodes during food availability, depression, and weight stigma in people experiencing FI. Stress may be another potential pathway.13–16 Previous studies among Latino populations residing in the mainland US have reported that food insecure individuals are more likely to experience higher levels of EE than food secure individuals.17 Food insecurity is a stressful life experience for a household, and evidence shows positive relationships with perceived stress.18 Additionally, studies support that individuals are more likely to change their eating behaviors during times of stress, and positive associations between stress and EE have been demonstrated.10 These dynamics are relevant to residents of PR, given the disparately high rates of FI and the fact that EE and UE have been linked to higher prevalence of chronic diseases.19 However, it remains unknown if this relationship upholds in the social context of PR, likely different than the US, including higher unemployment and poverty rates, racially-rooted structural barriers, gaps in healthcare services, and colonialist policies that have undermined the economy, political system, and health of the population.20–23

Given the aforementioned research gaps, this study aimed to assess the relationship between food insecurity and EE and UE among adults in PR. The role of perceived stress in this relationship as a potential mediator, and food assistance and the COVID-19 pandemic as potential moderators, were also explored. We hypothesized that FI is positively associated with both EE and UE, and that perceived stress would attenuate these associations.

## METHODS

### Study design

Data were obtained from the baseline examination of the PR Observational Study of Psychosocial, Environmental, and Chronic Disease Trends (PROSPECT) prospective cohort.24 PROSPECT was designed to estimate the prevalence of psychosocial, diet and food-related environment, and biological risk factors of cardiovascular diseases and other major chronic diseases among adults in PR. Participants were recruited using a multi-stage probabilistic sampling and community approaches since 2018. Probability sampling consisted of identifying potentially eligible participants using US Census block frames, then visiting these households for door-to-door enumeration. Community sampling included advertising the study at community locations and events, partner clinics, and social and mass media, and through referrals; this stage was predominant during COVID-19. To be eligible, individuals had to be 30-75 years at enrollment (chosen to detect cardiometabolic risk factors more likely to emerge at this age range),25–27 in a stable residence in PR for at least the previous year, and not planning to move away within the next 3 years. Individuals were excluded if they reported major psychiatric disorders or mental/physical disabilities that would prevent completion of an interview. Trained bilingual research assistants conducted standardized interviews and clinical examinations among participants that provided written informed consent.

The current study included participants recruited from March 21, 2019, to April 20, 2021. A total of 920 individuals provided written informed consent, and 19 were excluded due to incomplete interviews. Of the 901 participants, 865 provided complete information on either EE or UE from the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire R18-Version 2 (TFEQ-R18 V2).28 PROSPECT has full board review approval from the institutional review boards of Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Ponce Health Sciences University in PR, and University of Massachusetts Lowell. The study is registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03794531.

### Food insecurity

Food insecurity was measured by the three-stage 10-item USDA Adult Food Security Survey Module released in September 2012.29 This module has good sensitivity and specificity relative to the eighteen-item USDA Household Food Security questionnaire and was validated in Spanish.30 Using the previous 12 months as the reference period, the module calculated the severity of household FI by a total score that ranged from 0 to 10, with a higher score indicating more severe FI. A score of 0 was allocated as ‘high food security’, 1 or 2 as ‘marginal food security’, 3-5 as ‘low food security’, and 6-10 as ‘very low food security’. To maximize sample size, we included FI as a binary variable: participants with a score higher than 2 (i.e., low or very low food security) were categorized as experiencing food insecurity, and participants with a score equal or lower than 2 (i.e., high or marginal food security) were categorized as food secure.

### Emotional eating and uncontrolled eating

We measured EE and UE with the TFEQ-R18 V2, available in both English and Spanish.24 The EE and UE subscale consisted of 6 items each that evaluated eating in response to negative emotions (e.g., being anxious, wound up, depressed, lonely, sad, and nervous). Response options for all items were scored as follows: “definitely false” as 1, “mostly false” as 2, “mostly true” as 3, and “definitely true” as 4. To calculate the EE and UE final scores, responses of all items were summed and divided by the number of questions on a specific eating behavior to generate a mean score, with higher scores indicating greater EE or UE.

Since the continuous scores were not normally distributed, and transformation did not improve the normality, we categorized the participants according to the scores. Consistent with previous studies,17, 31 we included 3 categories: 1) no EE or UE, 2) moderate EE or UE, or 3) high EE or UE. The no EE and UE category comprised of individuals with a score of 1, thus answering “definitely false” to all items. The remaining score was divided by the median (2.00 for EE, 1.56 for UE), with moderate EE or UE being below or equal to the median and high EE or UE being above the median. Good reliability was shown in a previous study conducted among Latinx adults residing in the US, with a high Cronbach α coefficient (0.86).17

### Perceived stress

We also included a model with perceived stress as an additional covariate. The 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) was used to measure general perceived stress without referring to a specific source, and good reliability has been shown in previous studies, with the Cronbach α coefficient ranging between 0.7 and 0.9.32 This scale assessed the controllability and ability to cope with life events using the previous month as the reference period, with response options as “never,” “almost never,” “sometimes,” “fairly often,” and “very often.” The total score was summarized from the responses to all items, and the final score ranged from 0 to 40, with higher scores suggesting greater perceived stress.

### Demographics and covariates

Covariates included sex at birth, age, date of recruitment (before or after COVID-19 lockdown), ethnicity (self-reported from Puerto Rican, Dominican, US-American (non-Hispanic US-native), or Other), educational attainment, household size, household income, marital status, employment status, and participation in the Puerto Rico Nutrition Assistance Program (NAP).33 The study also probed for participation in the Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program, which was reported by few participants (<5%). Adjusting for WIC did not change the models and thus it was excluded from the final models. All covariates except for date of recruitment were selected a priori because of their known association with FI and dysfunctional eating behaviors34, 35 A dichotomous variable for date of recruitment before or after the COVID-19 lockdown in PR (March 16, 2020) was included because of evidence suggesting that individuals’ eating behaviors and FI status may change during the COVID-19.36, 37 Age and household size were used as continuous variables. Educational attainment was a categorical variable defined from the highest level of education attained. Ethnicity was categorized as “Puerto Rican” or “other”. Annual household income was categorized as “<$10,000,” “$10,000-$20,000,” and “>$20,000.” Current NAP participation was probed with a binary (yes/no) question. We did not adjust for body mass index in the models as it may be considered a potential mediator or an outcome in the FI and dysfunctional eating behaviors association; previous research has omitted it as well.38–40

### Statistical analysis

Sociodemographic characteristics and eating behaviors were contrasted by food security status using t-tests for continuous variables and Pearson’s chi-square tests for categorical ones. Cross-sectional multinomial logistic models were applied to estimate the odds (95% confidence interval) of having each of the dysfunctional eating behaviors by FI status, adjusting for sex at birth, age, date of recruitment, ethnicity, educational attainment, household size, household income, marital status, employment status, and NAP participation. A linear regression model was also included to assess the outcome using the continuous score of EE or UE. Perceived stress was included to a second model to probe for potential mediation. The potential effect modification by NAP and recruitment date regarding COVID-19 was examined by including an interaction term in the models. The statistical software STATA 16 (StataCorp, College Station, TX) was used for all analyses. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and all tests were two-sided.

## RESULTS

The majority of the sample (79.7%) was classified as food-secure, while 20.3% of participants experienced FI; prevalence of differentiated categories of food security were 64% for high, 16% for marginal, 12% for low, and 8% for very low. In the overall sample, 34% reported no EE, 38% had moderate EE, and 28% had high EE; prevalence of UE was 16% for none, 43% for moderate, and 42% for high. Mean (SD) age of the analytical sample was 54 (13.7) years, and the majority were women, with most participants being of Puerto Rican heritage (Table 1). In the sample, FI was less prevalent (9.6%) among participants recruited after the COVID-19 lockdown, compared with participants recruited pre-pandemic (27.9%). Compared to food-secure participants, a greater proportion of food-insecure participants had less than high school educational attainment. Food-insecure participants were more likely to earn less than $10,000/year compared with food-secure participants. In addition, a lower proportion of food-insecure participants were married or living with a partner compared to the food-secure ones; more food-insecure participants were unemployed and used NAP benefits. Furthermore, a larger proportion of food-insecure participants reported high EE (42.1%) and high UE (55.8%) compared with food-secure ones (24.9% and 37.9%, respectively).

In unadjusted models, FI was significantly associated with higher odds of EE (moderate and high) and UE (moderate and high) when compared with the no EE or UE reference group (Table 2). In adjusted linear models, a food insecure participant scored 0.32 points (95% CI: 0.15-0.49; p<0.001) higher in EE and 0.23 points (95% CI: 0.09-0.36; p=0.001) higher in UE from TFEQ, compared to a food secure participant. These associations were slightly attenuated, but remained statistically significant, after additionally adjusting for PSS. In adjusted multinomial logistic models, FI was associated with nearly 2 times the odds of moderate EE (OR=1.92, 95% CI: 1.19, 3.09) and nearly 3 times the odds of high EE (OR=2.85, 95% CI: 1.75, 4.64); for UE, FI was associated with almost 2 times the odds of moderate UE (OR=1.78, 95% CI: 0.90, 3.49) and 3.28 (95% CI: 1.70, 6.33) higher odds of high UE. After further adjusting for perceived stress, the estimates and significance were attenuated. However, FI remained significantly associated with high EE and high UE. We did not observe a significant interaction between NAP status and FI for EE (p = 0.55) or UE (p = 0.58), or between recruitment time and FI for EE (p = 0.81) or UE (p = 0.08).

## DISCUSSION

This study found that adults in PR who reported experiencing FI had a higher likelihood of engaging in 2 dysfunctional eating behaviors, EE and UE. A previous study among adults of PR reported 31.9% prevalence of FI, higher than our overall sample (20.3%) or for individuals recruited before the COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020 (27.9%).4 Food insecurity was less reported for participants recruited after the lockdown. The reason behind this difference is unclear but could be related to either recruitment strategies before versus after the lockdown (the latter shifting to community sampling) or to expanded economic or food assistance provided during the pandemic. Still, the COVID-19 pandemic did not moderate the observed associations between FI and the dysfunctional eating behaviors. Similarly, we evaluated NAP status as a potential effect modifier because program benefits help reduce FI,41 but there was no statistically significant interaction between NAP status and FI on dysfunctional eating behaviors. Furthermore, although we were unable to formally test the role of mediation given the cross-sectional design, the attenuated risk of EE and UE after adjusting for perceived stress may suggest a potential mediating role.

Although the literature remains scarce, our findings are consistent with studies showing that FI was associated with high levels of EE among African American women and Latinx populations residing in the US, and was positively associated with UE among older non-Hispanic White and Black adults.8, 9, 11, 17 Other studies have reported similar associations with other dysfunctional eating behaviors, such as binge eating, both among young adults with ethnically diverse background during the COVID-19 pandemic and in a sample primarily comprised of Latinos and in a sample of ethnically diverse participants.10, 14

One limitation of this study was its cross-sectional nature, which precludes from establishing causality. The small sample size prevented us from assessing differentiated categories of FI, which have shown dissimilar associations with nutrition-related outcomes.15, 16, 42, 43 Additionally, although we adjusted for age as a covariate, we did not explore differences between participants in specific age groups, who may experience FI and dysfunctional eating behaviors in distinct ways.44, 45 The generalizability of the findings might be limited to residents in PR given the unique socio-political context of the island. However, this limitation is offset by the sample strategy, and it is also a study strength given that this population remains largely underrepresented in research but has a high burden of health disparities and is disproportionately affected by FI. In addition, this study expanded the extant knowledge on FI and dysfunctional eating behaviors in a vulnerable population.

## IMPLICATIONS FOR RESEARCH AND PRACTICE

The public health field is shifting the focus from ‘food security’ to ‘nutrition security’ to ensure that the food to which people have access provides the necessary nutrients to sustain optimal health.46, 47 In this context, the diet of adults in PR has been deemed of low quality, with less than 10% of the population meeting the recommended intake for vitamin D, potassium, polyunsaturated fats, fruit, red/processed meats, sodium, and sugary beverages.48 Some of these foods have been correlated with dysfunctional eating behaviors.49, 50 Thus, addressing FI alone may not resolve dietary and behavioral concerns in the population. Following the pillars of the recent US National Strategy on Hunger, Nutrition, and Health,51 strategies could prioritize nutrition and food security in overall health. For research, this could include assessing nutrients implicated in the FI-eating behaviors link, an analytical gap of our study that subsequent ones could fill. For healthcare or public health practice, this could include screening for diet quality or nutritional status during FI evaluations using validated tools such as the USDA module.

At the policy level, NAP in PR receives fewer funds and benefits compared to its counterpart, SNAP, in the states of the union.52, 53 Although we did not observe statistical differences in FI and dysfunctional eating behaviors by NAP status, congressional action to expand NAP or convert it to SNAP might placate some of the mediating factors linking them (e.g., depression, stress, stigma). Enhancing resources and funding for commonly used non-government food assistance programs in PR (such as food pantries, churches, and community gardens) and easy-to-access locally-sourced food might target FI at the food system, community, and interpersonal levels. Concurrently, efforts to improve eating behaviors can be made across all levels of the socioecological model. Lastly, stress-reduction programs or education, such as mindfulness, physical activity, or sleep hygiene, may be promoted, based on our results suggesting a potential mediating role of stress.

In conclusion, FI is associated with higher likelihood of engaging in EE and UE. Identifying modifiable factors and mediators that contribute to the association will help design interventions to reduce the negative effects from FI and dysfunctional eating behaviors in this vulnerable population. Longitudinal studies are needed to further disentangle these dynamics and identify possible mechanisms. Furthermore, these data support prioritizing policies that address structural barriers for secure access to healthy foods, as well as food assistance programs in PR and in similar vulnerable populations, to alleviate FI and the potential consequences on dysfunctional eating behaviors.
